Grievousness
gree'vus-nes
n. (oppressiveness; the quality of causing grief or hardship; heavy affliction)
From grievous, Old French grever, to burden, from Latin gravare, to load, from gravis, heavy. Grievousness is weight — what is laid on a man until he cannot carry it.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah has the word twice, and both times it is a weight laid on people by somebody. The first is the woe on legislators: “Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed” (Isa 10:1). The grievousness is written and prescribed — it is legislation, drafted and filed, and the next verse names its victims: “To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey, and that they may rob the fatherless” (Isa 10:2). This is oppression conducted lawfully, with paperwork, and God pronounces woe on the drafters. The second occurrence is the weight of invasion: they fled “from the swords, from the drawn sword, and from the bent bow, and from the grievousness of war” (Isa 21:15). War has a heaviness of its own beyond the blades. Both uses are about a burden imposed rather than a sorrow that merely happens, and both have the same divine answer: God attends particularly to the burdened. “Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: the poor committeth himself unto thee; thou art the helper of the fatherless” (Psa 10:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines grievousness as oppressiveness; weight that gives pain; the quality of giving pain, grief or sorrow; and calamity, affliction.

GRIE'VOUSNESS, n.

1. Oppressiveness; weight that gives pain or distress.

Woe to them that write grievousness. Is. 10.

2. Greatness; enormity; atrociousness; as the grievousness of sin.

3. Pain; affliction; calamity. Grievous is from grever, to burden, from the Latin gravis, heavy.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 10:1 — "Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed;"

Isaiah 21:15 — "For they fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, and from the bent bow, and from the grievousness of war."

Isaiah 10:2 — "To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey, and that they may rob the fatherless!"

Psalm 10:14 — "Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: the poor committeth himself unto thee; thou art the helper of the fatherless."

Modern Corruption

Because the oppression Isaiah condemns is legal, it is the kind most easily defended — and the woe is pronounced on the drafters, not the enforcers.

expand to see more

Isaiah 10:1 is one of the few places Scripture pronounces woe specifically on lawmakers, and the offence is not lawlessness but law: decrees decreed, grievousness written and prescribed. Everything in verse 2 is done through channels. The needy are turned aside from judgment — that is, in court; the poor lose their right; widows become prey and the fatherless are robbed, all of it legally. This is the permanent answer to the claim that legality settles the moral question. A statute can be a sin, and the men who drafted it are named first.

The corruption in the other direction is a piety that reads Isaiah 10 as licence for the church to become a legislative faction, as though the prophet's remedy were better decrees. Isaiah's own remedy is the LORD's hand: Assyria is the rod in verse 5, and the rod is broken in its turn. And Psalm 10:14 supplies what no policy can — the poor committeth himself unto thee. Christians are to seek just laws, since the magistrate is God's minister for good; but a church whose whole answer to grievousness is legislative has forgotten who the helper of the fatherless actually is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew amal (H5999), toil, trouble, mischief; aven (H205), iniquity, trouble; koved (H3514), heaviness; Latin gravis, heavy.

expand to see more

Hebrew amal (H5999) — travail, trouble, mischief; Isaiah 10:1, what the scribes wrote.

Hebrew choqeqim chiqqe-aven (H2710, H205) — decreers decreeing decrees of iniquity; Isaiah 10:1, a threefold play on one root.

Hebrew koved milchamah (H3514) — the heaviness of war; Isaiah 21:15.

Hebrew gravis → Old French grever — to load, to burden; Webster's root, weight before sorrow.

Hebrew yathom (H3490) — the fatherless; Isaiah 10:2 and Psalm 10:14, the same party in the dock and in the refuge.

Usage

"“Write grievousness which they have prescribed” — oppression with paperwork."

"“Turn aside the needy from judgment” — done in court, done lawfully."

"“The grievousness of war” — a weight beyond the blades."
